To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) smart meters and intermittent capacities can be substitutes or complements depending on their relative cost and on the correlation existing between intermittents and demand and that (ii) smart meters are more likely to be used if the volatility of the spot price is higher.

the adoption of smart meters is optimal only if the volatility of the spot price is high, and that the adoption of intermittent capacities and smart metering are complements only if the correlation between intermittent energy and consumption is negative or if intermittent capacities are large enough.
the adoption of smart meters is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for a successful integration of intermittent electric generation technologies in the electric market.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optimal penetration of intermittent electric generation technologies and smart meters.
the optimal design of electric markets in which consumers are equipped with smart meters and producers are using intermittent technologies.

the question of whether smart meters are a substitute or a complement to renewable energy technologies, and we show that the answer depends crucially on the correlation between intermittent energy and electricity demand, as well as on the size of intermittent capacities.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in the absence of any policy measure, the optimal penetration of intermittent technologies is decreasing in the volatility of electricity price and in the cost of smart meters, and increasing in the correlation between demand and intermittent energy.
smart meters should not be seen as substitutes for intermittent technologies, but rather as complements, provided that the volatility of the spot price is large.
smart meters and intermittent technologies should not be seen as substitutes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
smart metering can be a useful complement to intermittent generation only if the intermittent capacity is not too large and if the correlation between intermittent energy and consumption is negative.
smart metering is a useful tool for managing the intermittence of electric production from renewable sources only if the cost for installing and operating smart meter is not too high.

the optimal penetration in smart meters is increasing when the volatility of the spot price increases, which is a direct consequence of the fact that smart meters are a tool to reduce this volatility.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the optimal penetration rate of intermittent technologies and smart meter is not necessarily increasing in the volatility induced by intermittent generation.
smart meters are not a panacea for reducing the costs of intermittent electric technologies.
, in the absence of a carbon tax or a cap-and-trade system on CO2 emissions, the adoption of intermittent technologies and smart metering should be analyzed jointly.
